summary_md: GCOMB (Manchanda et al., NeurIPS 2020) learns a heuristic for budget-constrained set problems on graphs: max coverage, max vertex cover and influence maximization. A GCN regresses probabilistic-greedy marginal-gain scores; a noise predictor prunes low-value nodes; then n-step Q-learning picks seeds using score plus locality, the count of neighbours not already covered. The payoff is speed, not quality. On small graphs greedy already reaches at least 99 percent of the CPLEX optimum (BP-500 at b=20: GCOMB 0.998, greedy 0.99, optimal 1). On real graphs GCOMB matches greedy and runs about 10 times faster, 2 to 4 times faster than CELF on YouTube, and 30 to 160 times faster than IMM. It still finishes on billion-edge graphs where IMM runs out of 256 GB RAM. The paper explicitly excludes sequential and capacity-constrained problems (Sec 5). For Paul's systems, the dashboard's budget max-coverage recruiter is the direct descendant. It keeps GCOMB's locality idea (count only newly covered members) and a degree prune, but it uses exact greedy, which this paper's own evidence supports on a 533-member graph. The paper does not support replacing the CELF joint optimizer or the lazy-greedy frontier with a learned policy. Its gains appear only at million-edge scale. The optimizer's per-member PMAX cap is the capacity constraint GCOMB excludes. The IM objective is single-colour IC, evaluated with 10,000 Monte Carlo runs, not the system's two-colour competitive cascade at MC 20. An online scan found a 2024 VLDB benchmark (Liang et al., arXiv 2406.14697) reporting that lazy greedy consistently beats five deep-RL methods, GCOMB included, on max coverage. IMM and OPIM beat them on IM in most settings. That benchmark is not in the vault.

bearings.paper_claim: Locality = neighbours not yet covered by the partial solution (Eq 3) and pruning of low-value nodes drive selection. Greedy reaches at least 99 percent of optimal on small graphs (Table 1b: BP-500 b=20 GCOMB 0.998, greedy 0.99, optimal 1). GCOMB matches greedy quality and wins only on time at scale.
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit is plain greedy max coverage. Each candidate's gain counts only newly covered probability mass, cov = 1 - prod(1 - p). Candidates below 0.1 x mean degree are pruned. The budget in $k becomes a seed count via K.CEDGE, so the constraint is uniform-cost cardinality. The template comment cites GCOMB for both ideas and says no ML is needed at this scale.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds while the graph is about 533 members and the objective is monotone submodular coverage. The live caller passes target -1, so the 1-1/e claim applies. The unused target branch multiplies gain by (1 + 2 dT) and would not carry it. The degree prune is a fixed rule, not GCOMB's learned noise predictor.

bearings.paper_claim: GCOMB's advantage is wall-clock speed on large graphs: 10x over greedy, a 4.0 to 2.01 speed-up over CELF on YouTube (1.13M nodes), saturating training in 10 minutes. Sequential and capacity-constrained problems are out of scope (Sec 5).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.2 Table 2b and Figs 2d-2e p.7; Sec 5 p.9
bearings.system_side: The joint optimizer is CELF lazy greedy over $500 concave chunks of a $2.5M pot. A per-member cap PMAX is $10k, and conversions rebuild the queue. This is a capacity-constrained allocation over about 533 members, not a set-selection problem on a large graph.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A learned GCOMB-style policy would apply only if the problem became pure set selection without per-member caps and the graph grew by orders of magnitude. At the current scale CELF is exact enough and fast. The 2024 VLDB benchmark (Liang et al.) finds lazy greedy beats GCOMB on max coverage.

bearings.paper_claim: IM experiments use single-colour Independent Cascade with spread from 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations. GCOMB matches IMM within small spread differences (Table 3a, largest about 3e-3) and is 30 to 160 times faster. It is defined for set problems, not sequential or routing ones.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.3 Table 3a p.8; App A; Sec 5 p.9
bearings.system_side: The frontier runs lazy greedy up to 60 seeds. Spread comes from a two-colour competitive cascade at MC 20 with common random numbers. The knee is the last seed whose marginal is at least a quarter of the peak marginal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's guarantees and comparisons assume submodular single-cascade IC. The competitive race with bystander mobilization need not be submodular. The paper offers no test of MC 20 adequacy; its own evaluation convention is 10,000 runs. An orienteering or political-capital route formulation is sequential, which GCOMB excludes.

gaps_exposed: No learned or sampled-greedy solver is needed at the 533-member scale, and none exists. If Melange ever runs IM on the staffer network or a larger person graph, the scaling evidence here (IMM out of memory at 256 GB on billion-edge graphs) becomes relevant.

The budget frontier's MC 20 spread estimate has no convergence check in this paper's terms (10,000 runs). CRN reduces variance in marginals, but the paper offers nothing on whether 20 runs rank seeds stably.

The template comment calls the budget mode cost-bounded. It is actually cardinality-bounded at uniform cost K.CEDGE. A heterogeneous per-member cost would need the cost-benefit greedy variant and its weaker bound.

The online scan found Liang et al. 2024 (VLDB, arXiv 2406.14697), A Benchmark Study of Deep-RL Methods for Maximum Coverage Problems over Graphs. Lazy greedy beats GCOMB on max coverage there, and IMM and OPIM beat it on IM in most settings. It is not in the vault and is a candidate to add.
flags: Paul's position on the joint optimizer expects a learned policy (GCOMB) to replace greedy at scale. The paper's own results show no quality gain over greedy, only speed on million-to-billion-edge graphs. An independent 2024 VLDB benchmark finds lazy greedy beats GCOMB on max coverage. This is not a brain-rule conflict, but the expectation is not supported at Melange's scale.

Paul's position on the budget frontier maps GCOMB budgets onto a political-capital orienteering formulation. GCOMB explicitly excludes sequential problems (Sec 5), so the paper does not ground that mapping.
No rejected SNA proposal is argued here: no cosponsorship-edge dropping and no per-edge volume normalization. No closeness or access-probability language transfers.
paul_alignment: There are no annotations on this file; Paul's positions come from component_literature. The pathfinding position, GCOMB pruning plus locality as grounding, agrees with the evidence and matches the code (make_dashboard_html_00.tpl:773-793). The joint-optimizer expectation that GCOMB should replace greedy at scale is stale for the system as built. At 533 members, CELF is already the right tool, the paper's own gains are speed-only and appear at 1M+ nodes, and the optimizer's PMAX cap is a capacity constraint GCOMB excludes. The budget-frontier orienteering reading goes beyond what the paper claims.

related.why: S2V-DQN is GCOMB's main learned baseline. GCOMB matches its quality on BP-2k (0.89 vs 0.87) and scales past the 20,000-node memory limit that stops S2V-DQN.
GCOMB's IM objective is the Kempe-Kleinberg-Tardos Independent Cascade spread and relies on its greedy 1-1/e guarantee.

It argues cheap centrality heuristics rival greedy IM. GCOMB instead argues learned heuristics match greedy faster. Both bear on whether the dashboard needs more than greedy plus PageRank (tpl:794-809).
RELINK moves deep-RL IM from node selection to edge activation in closed networks. The dashboard's closedCascadeRoute (tpl:828-831) uses that design rather than GCOMB's node-set framing.
Also learns an RL policy for influence maximization over graphs, but under unknown network structure rather than GCOMB's billion-edge scale.
RL for IM with contingent seed acceptance, which matches the system's seed gate more closely than GCOMB's deterministic seed set.
The system's cascade is the competitive two-colour IC from this work. GCOMB's single-colour IC results do not transfer directly.
